CSCI3130 Formal Languages and Automata Theory

Definitions

There are three key concepts: Language, Grammar and Automata. These are interrelated and are many equivalent concepts for them.

Language: a set of strings over an alphabet, where a string is a sequence over an alphabet.

Grammar: a set of variables, terminals and production rules to generate a language.

Automata: a machine to either (1, acceptor) accepts strings in a language, (2, generator) generates strings in a language or (3, transducer) transform the input string to an output string.

Finite Acceptor (Deterministic / Non-deterministic)

DFA / NFA can be defined as a 5-tuple $(Q, \Sigma, \delta, q_0, F)$, where $Q$ is the set of internal states, $\Sigma$ is the input alphabet, $\delta$ is the transition function, $q_0 \in Q$ is the initial state and $F \subset Q$ is the set of final states.

Transition graph can be built from DFA / NFA, and a string $w \in \Sigma^*$ is accepted iff there exists a walk with label $w$ from $q_0$ to any state in $F$. The only difference between DFA and NFA is the definition on the transition function: For DFA, $\delta$ is a total function on $Q \times \Sigma \rightarrow Q$, while for NFA, $\delta$ is a partial function on $Q \times \Sigma \cup \{\lambda\} \rightarrow 2^Q$.

NFA and DFA are equivalent: any DFA is also NFA, and any NFA can be converted to an equivalent DFA via Power Set Construction.

To minimise the number of states in a DFA, we may simply merge all non-distinguishable states.

Regular Expression / Grammar

Regular Expression: An expression built from (1) Primitives: $a \in \Sigma$, $\lambda$ and $\varnothing$; (2) Combine RE $r_1$ and $r_2$ via $r_1 + r_2$, $r_1 \cdot r_2$, $r_1^*$ and $(r_1)$.

RE is equivalent to NFA: Converting RE to NFA can be done by induction on operations, whereas converting NFA to RE can be done by repeatedly delete vertices from the Generalised Transition Graph (GTG).

Regular Grammar: $(V, T, S, P)$ where production rules $P$ is either right-linear or left-linear. Right-linear: all production rules are of the form $A \rightarrow w$ where $A \in V$, $w \in T^*(V \cup T \cup \{\lambda\})$.

Conversion between Regular Grammar and NFA are trivial by simply considering the variables in $V$ as states, and therefore we call the family of languages accepted by NFA / DFA, described by Regular Expression or generated by Regular Grammar as Regular Language.

Properties of Regular Language

Given Regular Languages $L_1$ and $L_2$, we know that languages $L_1 \cup L_2$, $L_1 \cap L_2$, $L_1 L_2$, $L_1^*$, $L_1^R$, $\bar{L_1}$ and $L_1 \setminus L_2$ are all regular as well. These can be proven from manipulations on the corresponding DFA, say setting $F$ to $Q \setminus F$, connecting the DFAs in some way or with the Product Construction.

Pumping Lemma: Given a Regular Language $L$, there exists a constant $m$ such that for all $w \in L$ with $|w| \ge m$, we can decompose $w$ into $xyz$ with $|y| \ge 1$ and $|xy| \le m$, where $xy^iz \in L$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. This can be proven via graph travesal on DFA with pigeonhole principle.

Context-Free Grammar

CFG are grammar where all production rules are in $V \rightarrow (V \cup T)^*$. That said, no context involved when in substitution. A language is called Context-Free iff it is described by some CFG.

For a derivation $S \Rightarrow^* w$ where $w \in T^*$ on a CFG, we can build a derivation / parse tree. The string $w$ is called to be yield from the CFG. Using leftmost/rightmost derivation can make derivation order unique.

A string $w$ is ambiguous if there are two different derivation trees for it, and a CFG is called inherently ambiguous if every string in it is ambiguous.

Backus-Naur Form: <expr> ::= <term> | <expr> + <term>. LL and LR grammar are special forms that can be parsed in linear time.

Given a CFL, there exists a CFG without $\lambda$-productions, unit-productions or useless-productions, which is done by simply removing them one-by-one.

Chomsky Normal Form (CNF): $A \rightarrow BC$ or $A \rightarrow a$. Trivial to compute from CFG, and exists $O(w^3)$ parsing algorithm (CYK, just Range DP).

Greibach Normal Form (GNF): $A \rightarrow aV_1V_2 \cdots V_k$ where $k \ge 0$. Not that trivial to compute, but help us to prove the equivalence of CFG and Non-Deterministic Pushdown Automaton.

Non-Deterministic Pushdown Automata

NPDA can be defined as a 7-tuple $(Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, z, F)$, where $\Gamma$ is the stack alphabet and $z$ is the stack start symbol, where other means the same as in DFA. Specifically, $\delta$ is a partial function on $Q \times \Sigma \times \Gamma \rightarrow 2^{Q \times \Gamma^*}$. A string is accepted iff there exists a computation that consumes all of input string and ends up in a final state. Formally, $L(M) = \{ w: (q_0, w, z) \vdash^* (q_f, \lambda, s)\}$.

CFG is equivalent to NPDA, by considering the Greibach Normal Form of the CFG and restricted form of NPDA.

DPDA is a restriction on NPDA where at each moment, at most one transition exists. This corresponds to Deterministic Context-Free Language.

Properties of Context-Free Language

Given CFLs $L_1$ and $L_2$, $L_1 \cup L_2$, $L_1 L_2$ and $L_1^*$ are CFLs as well. However, $L_1 \cap L_2$ is not guaranteed to be CFL, and this problem is undecidable. However, if $L_1$ is regular, $L_1 \cap L_2$ can be proven to be CFL via Product Construction.

Pumping Lemma: Given a CFL $L$, there exists constant $m$ such that for all $w \in L$ where $|w| \ge m$, we can decompose $w$ into $uvxyz$ where $|vxy| \le m$ and $|vy| \ge 1$, such that $uv^ixy^iz \in L$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. Linear CFL: We can enforce $|uvxyz| \le m$ as well.

Turing Machine

Standard Turing Machine can be defined as a 7-tuple $(Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, q_0, \square, F)$, where $\Gamma \supset \Sigma$ is tape alphbet, whereas $\square \in \Gamma \setminus \Sigma$ is the blank symbol. Specifically, $\delta$ is a partial function on $Q \setminus F \times \Sigma \times \Gamma \rightarrow Q \times \{\texttt{L}, \texttt{R}\}$. The input is written on the tape, no transition from final states allowed and the machine halts when no possible transition.

Turing Machine can act as an acceptor or a transducer. Formally, the accepted language is $L(M) = \{ w: q_0 w \vdash^* x_1 q_f x_2\}$, and the transduced output $f(w)$ is $q_0 w \vdash^* q_f f(w)$.

Variations on Turing Machine: Stay-Option, Semi-Infinite Tape, Off-Line, Multi-Tape, Multi-demensional, Non-determinstic. All can be simulated by the standard Turing Machine.

Universal Turing Machine: Simulate every other Turing Machine, by passing the transition and inital tape content of $M$ as input, and maintain states of $M$ as three tapes in Universal TM.

Linear-Bounded Automata: bounded to the input space, which is equivalent to Context-Sensitive Language, i.e., all production rules are non-contracting.

Recursive and Recursively Enumerable Languages

A language is Recursively Enumerable iff some TM accepts it, whereas a language is Recursive iff some TM accepts it and halts for every input. Easy to see that Recursive implies Recursively Enumerable, since we can simply loop through the strings in the countable set $\Sigma^*$ and check one-by-one. Since TM is countable and set of all languages is uncountable, there exists languages not recognisable by TMs.

Decidibility / Computability

There are a bunch of problems about TM are undecidible, i.e., there does not exists a generic algorithm to solve them. For example, the membership problem: Given a TM $M$ and a string $w$, decide whether $w \in L(M)$; or the halting problem: decide whether $M$ will ever halts; state-entry problem: whether TM will ever enter a state given a string $w$; blank-tape problem: whether TM will halt given a blank tape.

Uncomputable functions: Maximum number of moves for a TM that halts given a blank tape. We can reduce this to the halting problem.

Complexity Classes

We may define complexity classes for languages, determinstic or non-determinstic, respectively: DTIME($T(n)$) if there exists a deterministic multi-tape Turing Machine that accepts $L$ in $O(T(n))$, and NTIME($T(n)$) for non-deterministic multi-tape Turing Machine. We thus have $L_{REG} \subset $ DTIME($n$), $L_{CF} \subset$ DTIME($n^3$), where $L_{REG}$, $L_{CF}$, $L_{CS} \subset$ NTIME($n$).

We define $$\textbf{P} := \cup_{k \ge 1} {\text{DTIME(}n^k\text{)}}$$ and $$\textbf{NP} := \cup_{k \ge 1} {\text{NTIME(}n^k\text{)}}$$ As the two well-known complexity classes. Clearly $\textbf{P} \subset \textbf{NP}$, but it is unknown whether the subset relation is proper or not. Problems in $\textbf{P}$ are called tractable, i.e., sensible to be computed out, and intractable otherwise.

Polynomial-time Reducible: Two languages $L_1$, $L_2$ are polynomial-time reducible iff there exists a deterministic Turing Machine to transform $w_1$ to $w_2$ in polynomial time where $w_1 \in L_1 \iff w_2 \in L_2$. A language $L$ is $\textbf{NP}$-hard iff every other $\textbf{NP}$ language can be reduced to $L$, whereas a language that is both $\textbf{NP}$ and $\textbf{NP}$-hard is called $\textbf{NP}$-complete.
